To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the CRM1-recognizable NES is functional in normal cells but not in tumor cell, and that the tumor cell-specific NES is active only in tumor cells due to the action of the phosphorylation site adjacent.

the CRM1-recognizing nuclear export sequence (amino acid 97-105), located in the COOH-terminal tumor cell-specific nuclear localization signal (amino acids -3 to -9), is functional in normal cells, but is inactivated by phosphorylation of threonine 98.
the tumor cell-specific targeting of the apoptotic protein VP3 to the nucleus is modulated by CRM1-recognized export signal that is functional in normal cells but is inactivated in tumor cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of signals that are involved in the nucleocytoplasmatic trafficking of VP3.

the identification of the signals that control the nucleocytoplasmatic trafficking of the tumor cell-selective apoptosis inducer, apoptin, and the elucidation of their role in the tumor cell-specific apoptotic activity of apoptin.
the elucidation of the mechanisms of VP3 nucleocytoplasmatic trafficking and the identification of the signals that confer tumor cell-specific nuclear localization of VP3.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the tumor cell-specific targeting signal of apoptin consists of a nuclear retention sequence that functions as a nuclear targeting sequence in tumor cells and a CRM1-recognizable nuclear export signal which is active in normal cells.

VP3 is a tumor cell-specific nuclear protein that is exported from the nucleus by the action of a CRM1-dependent nuclear export signal, which is active in normal cells and is inhibited in tumor cells by the action of an adjacent phosphorylation site.
the nuclear accumulation of VP3 is modulated by the combined action of a tumor cell-specific nuclear localization signal, a CRM1-identified NES, and a nuclear retention sequence.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
tumor cell-specific nuclear accumulation of VP3 is modulated by the CRM1-recognizable NES which is active in normal cells but inactive in tumor cells.
the CRM1-recognizable NES is the major signal for the nucleocytoplasmatic trafficking of VP3, and the phosphorylation of threonine 98 is a key factor in regulating its nuclear export.

VP3 nuclear localization in normal cells is mediated through the combined actions of a leucine rich sequence and a CRM1-recognizable NES, whereas in tumor cells the CRM1-recognizible NES is inhibited through phosphorylation of threonine 105, allowing VP3 nuclear accumulation through the basic amino acid stretches in the COOH terminus of the protein.
The main takeaway from our work is that

tumor cell-specific nuclear localization of VP3 is not only dependent on the nuclear localization signal (NLS) in the VP3 NH2 terminus but also on a nuclear export signal (NES) within its COOH terminus.
tumor cell-specific nuclear accumulation of VP3 is dependent on a CRM1- recognized NES, which is active in normal cells but not in transformed cells.

VP3 is a unique example of an apoptin that is able to enter and accumulate in the nucleus of both normal and tumor cells, and that its nuclear retention is dependent on a leucine-containing sequence that is associated with promyelocyctic leukemia bodies.
